1:
The turn from the previous chapter strikes them first. Matthew Henry calls the connexion plain but very surprising: Jacob had just been said to refuse God's ways and to be stubborn under correction, so one would think God would abandon them, and instead the next words are fear not, I have redeemed thee. Charles Ellicott finds more in the title than the Maker of heaven and earth, since God created Israel as answering to an archetype in his own purpose; to call by name is everywhere, and pre-eminently in the East, the mark of an individualising tenderness, almost of a predestinating love.

Whether a new discourse begins here is left open. John Calvin says it is hard to tell, since the prophets did not divide their discourses in a way that shows what they spoke on any given day, but thinks this connected with what precedes, moderating the severity just used. John Gill rejects two identifications, Cyrus and the return, and the deliverance from the Assyrian, referring it to the Christian church. Adam Clarke reads it as predicting the time when God should gather Abraham's posterity from every quarter under heaven.

On the waters and fire the readings are historical or general. Ellicott takes the two elemental perils proverbially, for every form of danger. Gill reports a scheme from a father of the church: Jewish expositors made the waters the Egyptians, the rivers the Babylonians, the fire the Macedonians, the flame the Romans, which he calls not amiss while preferring afflictions in general. Keil and Delitzsch note only that a second causal particle introduces the ground of the promise securing them against either element. Calvin turns it into a warning: the Lord has not redeemed thee to enjoy pleasures or abandon thyself to ease, but that thou shouldest be prepared for enduring every kind of evil.

The ransom of Egypt is dated three ways. Clarke takes it of the Assyrian invasion, when the king was diverted from Jerusalem against Egypt, but grants reasonable objections and offers a general sense, that God has often saved his people at other nations' expense. John Wesley keeps the same event, naming the king who meant to revenge his father's disgrace. Ellicott looks the other way, painting God, after the manner of men, as surrendering Egypt and other kingdoms to Cyrus as a price paid for liberating the Jews of Babylon, and finds the fulfilment in the later Persian conquest of Egypt.

Being precious is denied as merit by all. Calvin reports the reading that makes it thou wast honourable because I raised thee to honour, but takes the clause as the reason God gave up Egypt: because I loved thee, therefore I gave a man for thee. By these words the prophet excludes all personal worth, that the people may not boast of merit, since the cause of salvation is the undeserved love of God. Gill says the same: they have no intrinsic worth, are of the same lump with others, precious neither in their own eyes nor the world's. Wesley dates the affection from the choosing.

The gathering from four quarters is read as geography and rhetoric. Ellicott shows the dispersion already wide in the prophet's day: the ten tribes carried to the cities of the Medes, the Babylonian exile begun, others beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, sons of Judah sold by Phoenician traders to the western isles; in the summons to north and south he hears an escort of honour given the returning exiles. Calvin says the four parts include the whole world, as in all languages, but the prophet speaks more loftily than the lawgiver, wishing the people to see the event as already done, God commanding every creature with supreme authority. Clarke parses the last verse's three verbs: created, produced out of nothing; formed, given the shape suited to his station; made, adapted to God's designs.
8:
Who the blind and deaf are comes first. Charles Ellicott hears the command come abruptly, as from a divine voice, a reversed echo of the previous chapter, where Israel saw but did not observe: here the blind and deaf, the heathen or the Israel fallen into heathenism, have capacities that will one day be developed. Adam Clarke takes them for the Gentiles, whose natural faculties, properly used, must have led them to the one true God, since his eternal power is clearly seen in his works and would have kept them from the folly of idols. John Gill lists older readings and settles on a summons to the heathen. Matthew Henry recalls the psalm where idols have eyes and see not, and those who make them are like them.

John Calvin finds the clause's brevity obscure. Some translate it that God will bring out the blind and him who has eyes, meaning both who see and who do not; some take it of men whose eyes are too dim to perceive the secrets of heavenly wisdom. On a careful survey he prefers to take the two phrases separately: I will bring out the blind, so as to restore sight to them, and the deaf, so that they shall recover their hearing.

The court scene is staged in detail. Gill has the nations gathered in an open court of judicature, that their whole strength might be united, the most cogent arguments produced, and all hear the cause fairly argued. Henry has the patrons of idolatry called to appear and defend their gods, God challenging them to produce such proofs of divinity as the redemption from Babylon furnished. Ellicott identifies the challenge as one made two chapters earlier: which of their gods foretold the former things, events then future that have now come to pass? Calvin warns how hard the argument is: it is easy to ascribe to God the glory of divinity but very difficult to claim it so exclusively that all false gods are reduced to nothing, and at the nation's ruin unbelievers applauded their gods as having vanquished the true one.

Who the servant is divides them three ways. Clarke separates the terms: the Israelites are the witnesses, the prophet the servant God had chosen. John Wesley offers Cyrus, an eminent proof of God's foreknowledge, or else the Messiah, the most eminent witness in this cause. Ellicott takes the whole people as collectively addressed under that title, their calling and election not cancelled and still to be fulfilled, since in the restoration they would be a living proof of the foresight granted to the prophets. Calvin says God separates himself from the multitude of idols and produces his own witnesses, lest he be thought of their class, while reproaching them indirectly if they will not declare what they know. Gill has Israel testify to the exodus foretold centuries ahead, and the apostles to the prophecies of Christ.

The eternity clause is the chapter's hardest, and Clarke says so. Was there a time when God was not? No; yet he says before me. Will there be a time when God will not exist? No; yet he says after me. He refers both to creation: before me no god created anything, nor was anything pre-existent but myself. Wesley makes the contrast simpler: the heathen gods neither had a being before God nor shall continue after him, and he notes the contempt in calling them formed gods at all. Calvin draws the inference the others leave implicit: he who has a beginning and is not from himself cannot govern what he did not create, so in declaring his eternity God reminds us the world is his workmanship. Keil and Delitzsch say the address closes by holding up once more the object and warrant of faith; Ellicott glosses the last clause as who shall turn it back, an echo from Job.
14:
Babylon is named here for the first time in this part of the book, as Charles Ellicott notes. He would render the second clause I will bring them all down as fugitives, and takes the margin's bars for a variant, defences in the sense of defenders. John Calvin makes the conqueror a subordinate: Cyrus will be but a hired soldier rendering services to the Lord for his people's delivery, and the prophet does not name him but speaks of the army under his command. He adds that the words address not only those who saw it done but all whom God wished to comfort with a hope they could not have conceived. Matthew Henry explains the repetition: the faith of God's people in Babylon was at so low an ebb that there needed line upon line.

The ships draw an excursus. Adam Clarke sets out Babylon's advantages, open to the Persian Gulf by a river navigable for large vessels and joined to the Tigris by a canal called the Royal River, drawing the produce of the country north as far as the Euxine and Caspian; the queen who founded that part of its greatness had improved the navigation herself. Ellicott hears the irony, rendering it into the ships of their shouting, the ships that used to echo with the exulting joy of sailors, the word chosen to suggest another kind of shout coming, the wailing cry of despair. John Wesley has the common people of Chaldea cry out as they flee from the Persians in ships.

The return is set out as a second exodus. Ellicott hears a distinct echo of the crossing narrative and of a psalm: the return from Babylon is a second exodus from another house of bondage, in which as in the first the horse and his rider are thrown into the sea. Keil and Delitzsch mark a second field of the redemption picture opening here. John Gill takes it practically: he who made a way in the Red sea could easily remove whatever lay in the way of this deliverance. Calvin makes it a duty: we are ungrateful if former benefits do not lead us to hope for the future. Ellicott and Wesley agree the quenching is a lamp-wick's.

Then they are told to forget it. Calvin explains that all the miracles of the first redemption were of little importance beside the more remarkable one soon to come, whose glory throws the former into the shade as the sun's brightness makes the stars disappear; yet the prophet does not mean the Jews should forget a benefit he had commanded them to publish in every age. Wesley says the same of a greater object: beside the inestimable mercy of sending the Messiah, all former deliverances are scarce worthy of remembrance. Gill takes the return from Babylon only as a type of the spiritual redemption. Clarke keeps it historical, the same power bringing them back, and calls that a new prodigy.

The beasts that honour God are read literally, then figuratively. Clarke calls the image elegant and highly poetical: God will give so abundant a supply of water to his people traversing the desert that even the wild beasts, the serpents and ostriches that haunt those arid regions, shall be sensible of the blessing and break into praise. Calvin defends the extravagance: amidst so desperate a condition it was proper that magnificent language should extol God's power, words supplying what seemed wanting in the reality, and he compares the song where the sea saw and fled and the mountains leaped like rams. Gill refuses the literal sense, taking the creatures for the Gentiles, compared to them for savageness and stupidity. Wesley allows the beasts cause to praise, if they had abilities. Calvin closes on the ground of it all: you shall be saved, because you cannot perish unless my glory perish.
22:
The abruptness raises a question of authorship. Charles Ellicott reports that it has led many critics to doubt the genuineness of these verses, and answers that their insertion by a later writer would be as hard to understand as their coming from the hand that wrote the glowing picture just before. His own solution is that the prophet's experience taught him there would be in the future, as in the past, a dark side as well as a bright: the mercies shown the exiles would be measured not by their merits but by God's goodness, and the worship of the restored people would be as meagre and unthankful as in his own time. Matthew Henry finds the charge doing two things at once: clearing God's justice in the captivity, since they had cast him off and must own it before they are fit for deliverance, and magnifying his goodness in delivering them all the same.

Whether the reproach can be true at all is John Calvin's question: why bring it against Jews who were evidently very careful to offer sacrifices according to the law? Some refer the words to the captivity, when they could not have sacrificed had they wished, since it was lawful nowhere but at Jerusalem; Calvin thinks it a general reproach. He adds that calling on God's name includes the whole of his worship, a part put for the whole, and that God elsewhere makes it the chief part, since having said he despises sacrifices he adds, call upon me in the day of trouble. Adam Clarke answers by weight of emphasis: the Jews were diligent in the external services, offering prayers and incense and sacrifices, but their prayers were not offered in faith and their oblations went more often to their idols, and the Hebrew idiom uses a general negative comparatively, as in I will have mercy and not sacrifice.

The clause about not being wearied is read as history and as generosity. Ellicott takes it to imply the suspension of sacrifice during the exile, God having imposed no such bond service nor wearied them with demanding incense while they were far from the temple to whose ritual it belonged. John Wesley makes it a comparison: God had not laid such heavy burdens on them, nor required such costly offerings as might make them weary, nor anything like what idolaters freely performed for their idols. John Gill keeps to the letter: the small cattle are the kids and lambs the law required morning and evening, the larger brought still less often, and the versions give rams, sheep and lambs; these went not to God but to their idols. Keil and Delitzsch print the sentence without comment.

The sweet cane is identified, then turned against them. Ellicott takes it for a spice of the anointing oil, distinguished from the incense, and hears the previous verse's verbs repeated with the emphasis of scorn, the people having made their hypocritical worship a service their God had to endure until he was altogether weary of it. Gill has them think the calamus too expensive and leave it out, and reports two rabbis at odds, one saying they need not buy it since it grew plentifully in the land, the other answering better that it was not to be had there. Calvin identifies the same ingredient of the ointment with which the priests, the tabernacle and the ark were anointed, and gives God's reply: though thou buy cane for me with money, thou oughtest not to reckon that an expense bestowed on me. They lost their pains in all those ceremonies, he says, because they did not look to the proper end, exercising no faith. Wesley puts the reversal plainly: thou hast been niggardly in my service while sparing no cost for thine idols, and hast made me bear the load and burden of thy sins.
25:
The doubled pronoun is pressed by one of them. Adam Clarke calls the original extremely abrupt, three words meaning I, I, He, and asks whether there is any mystery in the form, whether it refers to a plurality of persons in the Godhead. John Calvin hears in the repetition a sharper rebuke of men's ingratitude, who rob God of the honour belonging to him alone, and takes the exclamation as a boast of his right to blot out the iniquities of a people who have no merits. Charles Ellicott notes the same figure in the first chapter and offers the resemblance as evidence of identity of authorship: there too the words that prove Israel's guilt are followed by the fullest offer of pardon. John Gill reads the blotting as the striking of a debt book, since sins are debts the sinner cannot pay. Clarke adds that in pardoning sin God can draw no reason but from his own goodness.

What God asks to be reminded of is disputed. Ellicott sets out the two supplements: remind me, if thou canst, of thy merits; or remind me of my promise to thee, of the electing grace that called thee to be my servant. The first, he thinks, fits better with what follows. Keil and Delitzsch take it the same way and make the scene forensic, since justice accuses and grace acquits, the question being whether Israel has actual merits on which justice would be obliged to pronounce it just. Calvin turns it into an offer: because men's pride cannot easily be corrected, God gives them liberty to argue what they please — if thou thinkest me forgetful, tell it thyself; remind me, if thou canst allege anything good; speak in thy turn, and I shall be silent. John Wesley answers in a line: God remembers nothing by which they have deserved his favour.

Who the first father was divides them five ways. Gill lists Adam, in whom all have sinned; Abraham, in whom they trusted, a sinful man though a great believer; Terah the idolater; and some particular king. Clarke quotes a rabbi for Adam: how can they say they have not sinned when their first father sinned and man has sin impressed on him through natural generation? Ellicott counts five readings — Adam, Abraham, Jacob, the ancestors collectively, or some high priest — and prefers Jacob. Calvin reports that almost all understand Adam, notes that some prefer Abraham, and quotes a rabbi who paraphrases the clause of Abraham's question how he should know he would inherit — not likely, he remarks, to strike a modern reader as the best proof that so holy a man was not perfect. Delitzsch rules Adam out on principle: Adam was forefather of the human race, not of Israel, and his debt was mankind's, so the reference must be to Abraham.

The teachers and profaned princes close the chapter. Ellicott renders the word literally as interpreters or mediators, used elsewhere of ambassadors, standing here for the priests and prophets who ought officially to have expounded the divine will; the curse he identifies as the ban answering to the anathema. Wesley agrees: if the people's intercessors were transgressors, the people had no reason to fancy themselves innocent. On the last verse Clarke emends, reading with the Syriac and Greek that thy princes have profaned my sanctuary rather than that God profaned the princes, and adds a lament over the curse they bear still. Delitzsch rejects the future pointing the old paraphrase introduced and takes the holy princes for the hierarchs, the supreme spiritual rulers as against the temporal. Calvin runs the other way, preferring a future sense so as to apply the words to the captivity still ahead, while allowing they may extend to calamities already suffered. Gill has the priesthood and its honour taken away, the daily sacrifice ceasing.
